newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to debate producer-distributor agreements.
newsitem.headline: EU to debate producer-distributor agreements.

text.p: The European Commission launched a debate on Wednesday on ways to ensure that agreements between producers and distributors in the European Union are not anti-competitive.
Because the debate has just begun, it said it would extend rules allowing British breweries and the oil industry to run exclusive distribution and purchasing agreements until December 31, 1999.

The Commission also announced it was planning to change the way it applied its ban on cartels to "agreements of minor importance". It proposed that accords be exempted from the rules on the basis of market share alone, rather than on turnover and market share as now.

The Commission said in a statement that it needed to rethink its policy toward producer-distributor agreements, or "vertical restraints", to take account of major changes in distribution methods and current economic thinking.
Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told a news conference the Commission had prepared a "green paper" outlining four possible options and was looking for input from interested parties.

An EU treaty provision barring anti-competitive agreements had been applied to vertical restraints relatively strictly -- to promote both "intraband" competition involving one brand and "interbrand" competition involving different brands, it said.

But the Commission has granted "block exemptions" allowing British breweries to operate tied pubs and oil companies to conclude exclusive purchasing agreements with petrol stations. Those were originally due to expire at the end of 1997.
Another block exemption which applies to franchising agreements -- which have mushroomed in the past 10 years in the clothing, perfume and hotel industries -- is due to expire at the end of 1999.
The Commission said it had received complaints that the current system was too rigid and put too much emphasis on the analysis of clauses rather than on the economic impact of the agreements.
Critics said, for example, that one non-exemptible clause should not void an entire exemption.

The green paper's options include keeping the current system, making block exemptions more flexible, limiting block exemptions to companies whose market shares are less than 40 percent and allowing parties with less than a 20 percent market share to claim a "presumption" of compliance with EU rules.

On the cartel ban, the Commission said it wanted to exempt "horizontal" accords -- involving companies operating at the same level of production and marketing -- if the combined market share was less than five percent.
"Vertical" agreements, involving companies at different economic levels, with less than a 10 percent market share would also be exempted.

Present rules exempt companies with a combined market share of less than five percent and joint turnover of less than 300 million Ecus ($357 million). The Commission said it would finalise its plan after a two-month comment period.
